title: Harvey Launches Legal Agent Bench (LAB) — Open-Source Benchmark for Autonomous Legal Agents
author: Artificial Lawyer · Harvey

dom.t: Professional tasks: Partial credit overstates complete success

st.t: Professional tasks: Partial credit overstates complete success
st.an: The source supports realistic, task-specific legal-AI evaluation by presenting LAB as a benchmark of agents completing multi-step, real-world legal work products rather than relying on exam performance or general model comparisons. It also supports reproducibility and scrutiny through open testing and rubric auditing, though it reports benchmark design rather than performance results and does not address the partial-credit/completion gap.
qs: It evaluates agent performance on real-world legal tasks using a structure of instructions, client matters, and required work product,’ the company explained.

kp.k: LAB benchmarks legal agents rather than standalone AI outputs
kp.d: The article announces Harvey’s Legal Agent Bench (LAB) on 6 May 2026, distinguishing it from Harvey’s Big Law Bench for testing AI outputs. The reported first version contains more than 1,200 agent tasks across 24 legal practice areas, evaluated against over 75,000 expert-written rubric criteria. These figures describe benchmark scope; the article reports no agent performance scores or measured reliability findings.
qs: Think of Harvey’s ‘Big Law Bench’ for testing AI outputs, now think of something made to measure the performance of agents.
The first version of LAB includes more than 1,200 agent tasks across 24 legal practice areas, and is evaluated by over 75,000 expert-written rubric criteria.

kp.k: Agent tasks combine planning, interaction and adaptation
kp.d: Harvey’s Head of Applied Research, Niko Grupen, describes agents decomposing and executing tasks, using data and tools, interacting with other agents, and asking humans for help and review. His M&A example involves identifying provisions in synthetic data, assessing their importance and writing a report. He also says issues have been deliberately inserted into test materials to see whether agents detect them. This describes capabilities being tested, not demonstrated successful performance or wholly unsupervised legal work.
qs: Grupen said it’s useful to think of agents as working across three main areas: planning, interacting, and adapting.

‘Agents will decompose a task, execute it, interact with data, tools, and also with other agents, and humans to ask for help and review. There is also adaptation where the agent may need to know more information,’ he said.
As Grupen explained, it could be an M&A deal, and the agent has to find key provisions in synthetic data, consider those provisions’ importance, and then write a report.
He noted that they have also added issues in the test material to see if the agents will spot them.

kp.k: Open benchmarking invites shared legal evaluation standards
kp.d: Harvey presents LAB as an open-source framework through which model providers, builders, researchers and the legal community can measure progress on legal tasks structured around instructions, client matters and required work product. The company invites law firms and other participants to audit rubrics, improve the harness and contribute task families. Grupen says participants can test Harvey agents or customized agents, including those built by vibe-coders.
qs: First, it will be opensource and open for everyone to get their agents tested.

Therefore ‘LAB provides a shared framework for model providers, agent builders, researchers, and the legal community to measure and track progress. It evaluates agent performance on real-world legal tasks using a structure of instructions, client matters, and required work product,’ the company explained.

‘We want model providers, startups, researchers, legal AI companies, and law firms to run the benchmark, audit the rubrics, improve the harness, contribute new task families, and help define what legal agent evaluation should measure next’, added Harvey.
He also noted that people can test out Harvey agents, or ones they’ve customized, and he underlined that they will welcome vibe-coders to test agents out on the open sourced LAB.

kp.k: Collaborators support evaluation; comparative rankings are forthcoming
kp.d: The article reports launch support from Nvidia, OpenAI, Anthropic, Mistral and DeepMind. Harvey states that collaborating research groups have already contributed to the benchmark and its research directions, with work covering open- and closed-source legal agents. A leaderboard is promised in the coming weeks to compare systems’ suitability for particular agentic tasks; no comparative rankings are supplied in this document.
qs: Enter Legal Agent Benchmark by Harvey, which launches with the support of a list of major names such as Nvidia, OpenAI, Anthropic, Mistral, and DeepMind.
There will also be a leader board in the coming weeks, so that you can see which AI systems are best at supporting certain agentic tasks.

Harvey added: ‘For the collaborators listed we are working closely with the foundation model labs, inference providers, Neo labs, and AI companies to evaluate the best open and closed source legal agents. These research groups have already made contributions to the benchmark and the research directions that it enables.’

kp.k: Legal agent impact is predicted through coding analogy
kp.d: The author predicts that agents will become a key part of legal technology and reports Grupen’s analogy with coding agents’ improvements and impact on engineering. The author further argues that public testing can build confidence, help lawyers develop use cases and increase familiarity. These are forward-looking and adoption-oriented arguments, rather than reported findings about legal productivity, employment or service quality.
qs: Yes, agents are going to become a key part of legal tech.
The tech is improving and as Grupen told AL, where coding agents have massively improved and had a big impact on engineering, so too legal agents will have a big impact here.
Allowing public testing of agents like this encourages faith in such products and helps lawyers to develop use cases and build familiarity with this approach.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Artificial Lawyer predicts that agents will become a key part of legal technology and reports Niko Grupen's prediction of a substantial impact on legal work, analogous to coding agents' impact on engineering.
pts.d: The article presents this as a forward-looking claim about legal agents, not a demonstrated labour-market or productivity result. It does not specify employment effects, cost reductions, or the extent to which agents will replace rather than assist lawyers.

pts.k: Harvey claims LAB supplies a shared framework for measuring legal agents' performance and tracking progress across legal tasks.
pts.d: Harvey describes a benchmark organised around instructions, client matters and required work product. Grupen describes agents as planning, executing, interacting and adapting, including asking humans for help and review. The M&A example involves finding provisions in synthetic data, assessing their importance and producing a report. These are descriptions of benchmark tasks and intended agent workflows, not reported evidence that agents successfully complete them. The proposed workflow allows human involvement rather than requiring fully unsupervised reliance on output.

pts.k: Artificial Lawyer claims that public agent testing encourages trust and helps lawyers identify use cases and become familiar with agentic workflows.
pts.d: The article links open testing to adoption-related benefits. It also anticipates a leaderboard enabling comparison of AI systems on particular agentic tasks. No observed changes in lawyers' trust, familiarity or adoption are reported.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source offers benchmark-design details and Harvey's research leadership as the basis for its evaluation claims; the broader impact prediction rests on an analogy to coding agents.
pts.d: The article reports more than 1,200 tasks, 24 practice areas and over 75,000 expert-written rubric criteria, alongside Grupen's account of task design and deliberately inserted issues. Harvey reports collaborator contributions. These establish the described scope and design of LAB, distinct from Harvey's Big Law Bench, rather than actual agent performance. The source supplies no benchmark scores, comparative results, reliability measurements or empirical evidence for the predicted impact or trust benefits.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The report is dated 6 May 2026; it describes LAB's initial release and a leaderboard expected within weeks, but gives no deadline for agents' wider legal impact.
pts.d: The source describes LAB as launching while using future tense for open-source availability. The broader impact claim is linked to improving technology, and the trust and familiarity claim is conditional on public testing. The described agent workflow permits escalation to humans for help and review. No date is specified for mature autonomous legal services or widespread adoption.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The direct beneficiaries identified are legal-agent developers, model providers, researchers, legal-AI companies, law firms and lawyers.
pts.d: Developers and researchers are invited to test agents, audit rubrics and contribute to the evaluation framework; this includes Harvey agents, customised agents and agents built by vibe-coders. Lawyers are expected to gain familiarity and develop use cases. The task coverage spans 24 practice areas, with M&A as an illustration. The associate comparison explains task delegation, not a specific prediction of associate displacement. The source does not identify particular effects on clients, access to justice, fees or firm staffing.
